explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. David says, "Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!" (Psalm 133:1). Notice he doesn't say it's tolerable or manageable. He says good AND pleasant, both at once. That's a rare combo, like a cookie that's warm and still holds its shape.

explanations.answer: Brothers living each on his own
explanations.explanation: Close to the idea, but the verse goes the other way. David says it's good and pleasant when brothers live together in harmony (Psalm 133:1). The word is "together," so it's about sharing the same space, not each one in his own corner. I've had a whole counter to myself before, and I can tell you it gets quiet fast.

Rules never come up in this verse, friend. David says the good and pleasant thing is brothers living together "in harmony" (Psalm 133:1). He's pointing at how they live together, not at a rulebook hanging on the wall. Harmony is the whole point here.

explanations.answer: Over the collar of his robes
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The oil runs "over the collar of his robes" (Psalm 133:2). It doesn't stop at the beard. It keeps on going, and that's the picture David wants us to see. I think that's one generous pour.

explanations.answer: All the way down to his feet
explanations.explanation: That's a long trip for oil, friend, and the verse doesn't send it that far. It says the oil runs down Aaron's beard "over the collar of his robes" (Psalm 133:2). That's where David stops the picture. Feet never come up.

Nice try, but the verse never puts the oil on the ground. It says the oil runs down on the beard, then "over the collar of his robes" (Psalm 133:2). The picture ends at the collar. If it hit the floor, somebody would be reaching for a mop, and nobody in this psalm is.

Yes, friend. David says it's good and pleasant when brothers live together in harmony, and then he says, "It is like fine oil on the head…" (Psalm 133:1-2). The oil is his picture of that harmony. He explains it with something you can almost see and smell.

This one's actually true, friend. David first says how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony (Psalm 133:1). Then he says, "It is like fine oil on the head, running down on the beard, running down Aaron's beard…" (Psalm 133:2). The oil is the picture, and harmony is what it shows.

That's right, baker. In the first picture the oil runs down from the head to the beard (Psalm 133:2). In the second, the dew of Hermon is "falling on the mountains of Zion" (Psalm 133:3). Both of them come down from above. David painted two pictures with one motion.

Look again, friend, because both pictures come down. The oil is "running down on the beard" (Psalm 133:2). The dew of Hermon is "falling on the mountains of Zion" (Psalm 133:3). Down in the first one, down in the second. I'd stand under that dew all day.

That's it, friend. "For there the LORD has bestowed the blessing of life forevermore" (Psalm 133:3). Forevermore is a big word, and David just sets it down quietly at the end. The LORD is the one who bestowed it.

explanations.answer: The blessing of victory in battle
explanations.explanation: A good guess, since David was a king who knew battles. But this verse names a different blessing: "the blessing of life forevermore" (Psalm 133:3). Battles don't come up in this psalm at all. It's all oil, dew and brothers together.

explanations.answer: The blessing of a great name
explanations.explanation: David had a great name, so I get the guess. But the verse says the LORD bestowed "the blessing of life forevermore" (Psalm 133:3). Nothing about a name is mentioned there. Life forevermore is the blessing on the table.

You've got it, baker. The song says, "Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD!" (Psalm 134:1). The call goes out to the night servants in particular. They're invited to come and bless Him.

explanations.answer: Come and rest from their work
explanations.explanation: Rest sounds nice at that hour, friend, and I'd take it. But the verse doesn't say it. The call is, "Come, bless the LORD…" (Psalm 134:1). Resting never comes up in this song.

explanations.answer: Come and keep watch at the gate
explanations.explanation: Watching the gate is a fine job, but it's not in this verse. The song calls out, "Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD!" (Psalm 134:1). The job is to bless the LORD. Gates aren't mentioned.
Right on, friend. The song says, "Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD!" (Psalm 134:2). The hands go up and the blessing goes to the LORD. Simple as that.

I can see why you'd think of the sky, with all those night hours. But the verse says, "Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD!" (Psalm 134:2). The sanctuary is where the hands are lifted, and the eastern sky doesn't appear.
Walls aren't in this song, friend. It says, "Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD!" (Psalm 134:2). The sanctuary is the direction. I'd say the walls can stay out of this one.

That's right, baker. The last line says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). The song opened by telling servants to bless the LORD, and it closes with the LORD blessing you. The blessing comes from Him.

No prophet shows up in this song, friend. The last line says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). The LORD Himself is the one blessing. That's a pretty good source.

David is a king, and he's the one who wrote the first song in this passage, so I see the thinking. But the last line of Psalm 134 doesn't name a king. It says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). The blessing comes from the LORD.
Yes, friend. "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). Zion was also where the dew fell in David's picture (Psalm 133:3). Two songs, one place.

Bethel is a real place in the Bible, but it isn't in this song. The last line says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). Zion is the place named. Zion also appears in the song before this one (Psalm 133:3).

Sinai is a mountain in the Bible, and I get why it came to mind. But this song says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). Zion is the place named here. It's the same Zion from the dew in the song before it (Psalm 133:3).
